Delta beats on quarterly results and raises full-year guidance

Published 2026-10-06 21:15 UTC

Delta Air Lines reported third-quarter earnings that beat analyst estimates and raised its full-year profit forecast, citing strong demand for premium seats and lower jet fuel costs. Adjusted earnings came in at $2.10 a share on revenue of $15.9 billion, compared with Wall Street expectations of $1.95 a share on $15.6 billion.

Premium cabin revenue grew 9% from a year earlier, outpacing main cabin sales, which rose 2%. Executives said travelers continue to pay for extra legroom and lounge access even as some budget-conscious customers cut back. Loyalty program revenue, including payments from the airline's credit card partner, rose 8%.

Fuel costs fell 12% compared with last year, helping operating margins expand to 13.5%. The airline said it expects its fuel price per gallon to stay roughly flat in the fourth quarter, though a recent rise in crude prices adds uncertainty.

Delta now expects full-year adjusted earnings of $7.10 to $7.40 a share, up from a prior range of $6.75 to $7.25. The company also said it would accelerate debt repayment and restore its dividend to pre-pandemic levels next year.

Executives said international travel remained strong, particularly to Europe and Asia, and that corporate travel bookings had improved for the third straight quarter. They warned, however, that capacity growth across the industry could weigh on fares on some domestic routes during the winter, when demand is usually softer.

The airline also addressed operational reliability after a series of technology problems last year. It said on-time arrival rates improved to 84% in the quarter and that it had invested in backup systems for crew scheduling. Shares of Delta rose 5% in morning trading, and other airline stocks also gained.

Analysts at several brokerages raised their price targets on Delta after the report, citing the strength of premium demand and the airline's improving balance sheet. Some cautioned that a slowing economy could hit leisure travel first, but said Delta's wealthier customer base gives it more protection than budget carriers.
